name: The Illusory Truth Effect
statement: Repeat a claim often enough and it starts to feel true, whether or not it is.
meaning: The illusory truth effect is the tendency to judge information as true simply because it has been encountered before. Repeated exposure raises the felt truthfulness of a statement regardless of whether it is actually true or false. Hearing or reading the same claim again and again nudges us toward believing it, so mere familiarity, not evidence, does much of the work of persuasion.
mechanism: The leading explanation is processing fluency. Each repetition makes a statement easier to read, understand, and retrieve, and the mind misreads that ease as a signal of truth, treating familiarity as a cue for reliability. Because the fluency comes from having seen the claim before rather than from any check of the facts, the sense of truth attaches to true and false statements alike. Even prior knowledge offers only partial protection, so a repeated falsehood can gain ground even against what we know.

examples.text: Hasher, Goldstein, and Toppino found in 1977 that repeated obscure trivia statements were rated truer over successive sessions, for both true and false items, while non-repeated ones were not.
Repeating a false claim in advertising, propaganda, or online rumour raises its later perceived truth, which is why debunking that needlessly restates a myth can backfire.
Later work showed repetition raised belief even in claims that contradicted what participants knew, so knowing the right answer does not fully block the effect.

variants.name: Processing fluency
variants.text: The dominant account that the ease of processing a repeated statement is misattributed as evidence of its truth, the mechanism behind the effect.

variants.name: The plausibility nuance
variants.text: Research suggesting repetition raises perceived truth even for implausible claims, though the size of any plausibility moderation, and whether it is a real effect or a measurement artifact, remains debated.

whyItMatters: It is central to understanding why misinformation and propaganda spread and stick, showing that sheer repetition, not evidence, can shape belief. It matters for advertising and marketing, for media literacy, and for the design of fact-checking, since it warns that restating a falsehood, even to correct it, can later make it feel truer. It reframes persuasion as partly a matter of exposure.

working.text: treat a claim's familiarity as no evidence of its truth, since repetition alone can manufacture the feeling of believability.
when correcting a myth, avoid needlessly repeating the false claim, which can raise its later perceived truth.
in communication, repeat accurate information rather than the falsehood, so fluency works for truth rather than against it.

limits: It is a robust, widely replicated effect, but its scope carries nuance. Prior knowledge provides only partial protection, not immunity, and whether it operates equally for firmly known falsehoods and how plausibility moderates it remain matters of genuine debate, with some apparent moderation possibly a measurement artifact. The processing-fluency account is the leading explanation rather than a settled certainty, and effect sizes vary across statements and settings.
misreadings: It does not work only on false statements; repetition raises the perceived truth of true and false claims alike, as the original study showed. Knowing the correct fact does not make you immune, since knowledge is only partial protection. And it is not confined to gullible people or plausible claims; the evidence indicates it operates broadly, even for implausible statements, though its strength varies.
origin: First identified by Lynn Hasher, David Goldstein, and Thomas Toppino in a 1977 study in the Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, and extended by later work, notably Fazio and colleagues, on how knowledge and plausibility interact with it.

sources.text: Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, "Frequency and the conference of referential validity," Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior 16 (1977): 107-112. — the original demonstration.
Illusory truth effect, Wikipedia. — the effect, the processing-fluency mechanism, and the knowledge and plausibility nuances.
